claim: Atoh7−/− mutant mice lack RGC inputs to visual thalamus
source: Using Atoh7−/− (also called Math5−/−) mutant mice, which lack RGC inputs to visual thalamus (Figure 1A), we previously reported a significant reduction in the number of interneurons in visual thalamus (Su et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and confirmed by the schematic in Figure 1A

claim: There is a significant reduction in Gad1+ neurons in both dLGN and vLGN of Atoh7−/− mice
source: Here, we demonstrate this loss using in situ hybridization (ISH) for Gad1 mRNA, which encodes for glutamic acid decarboxylase 67 (GAD67), an enzyme required for the production of GABA. This confirmed significant reduction in Gad1+ neurons in both dLGN and vLGN (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: Demonstrated by ISH data shown in Figure 1B-C with quantification

claim: The reduction in Gad1+ cells in Atoh7−/− vLGN is less striking than in dLGN because most Gad1+ cells in vLGN are principal projection cells and not local interneurons
source: It is important to highlight that the reduction in Gad1+ cells in Atoh7−/− vLGN is less striking than in dLGN, since most Gad1+ cells in vLGN are principal projection cells and not local interneurons.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on knowledge of cell types in vLGN

claim: Calb2Cre mice show widespread expression of Cre in the GCL of the retina as early as P0
source: We crossed mice carrying the Rosa26floxstop-TeNT allele with Calb2Cre mice, in which most, if not all, RGCs express Cre recombinase (Kerr et al., 2019; Sando et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2008) and widespread expression of Cre occurs in the GCL of the retina as early as P0 (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by citations and confirmed by imaging data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A

claim: Rosa26floxstop-TeNT;Calb2Cre mice show a significant increase in the area occupied by inputs from both eyes in dLGN
source: In Rosa26floxstop-TeNT;Calb2Cre mice, we observed a significant increase in the area occupied by inputs from both eyes, a hallmark of impaired activity-dependent RG refinement (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D, E).
evidence: Demonstrated by CTB labeling experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D, E

claim: Rosa26floxstop-TeNT;Calb2Cre mutants had impaired escape responses to looming stimuli
source: In contrast, Rosa26floxstop-TeNT;Calb2Cre mutants had impaired escape responses, indicating deficits in their ability to identify visual stimuli, although it is important to note that these responses were not as impaired as observed in Atoh7−/− mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, C).
evidence: Demonstrated by behavioral testing shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, C

claim: Impairing retinal activity had little impact on interneuron recruitment into visual thalamus
source: Surprisingly, in dLGN and vLGN, we did not observe a significant difference in the percentage of Gad1-expressing cells between the controls and mutants, revealing that decreasing retinal activity, or at least glutamate release by RGCs, had little impact on the recruitment of interneurons into visual thalamus (Figure 1E, F).
evidence: Demonstrated by ISH for Gad1 in Rosa26floxstop-TeNT;Calb2Cre mice shown in Figure 1E, F

claim: RGCs generate and secrete SHH
source: SHH signaling widely regulates FGF15 expression in the embryonic brain (Ishibashi and McMahon, 2002; Martinez-Ferre et al., 2016; Saitsu et al., 2005) and RGCs have been reported to generate and secrete SHH (Dakubo et al., 2008; Peng et al., 2018; Traiffort et al., 2001; Wallace and Raff, 1999), suggesting that SHH might regulate FGF15 expression and interneuron migration into visual thalamus.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous literature

claim: Shhfl/flNesCre mutants survive gestation but die by P18
source: As previously reported, Shhfl/flNesCre mutants survive gestation, however, die by P18 (Machold et al., 2003; Xu et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: There is a significant and dramatic decrease in the percentage of Gad1-expressing neurons in dLGN and vLGN of Shhfl/flNesCre mutants
source: In dLGN and vLGN of these mutants, we observed a significant and dramatic decrease in the percentage of Gad1-expressing neurons (Figure 1H, I).
evidence: Demonstrated by ISH data shown in Figure 1H, I

claim: Loss of SHH signaling in Shhfl/flNesCre mice results in a reduction in Fgf15 expression
source: Furthermore, loss of SHH signaling in Shhfl/flNesCre mice resulted in a reduction in Fgf15 expression, similar to what was observed in mice lacking retinal inputs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: Demonstrated by ISH data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C

claim: SHH signaling is critical for both thalamic Fgf15 expression and the recruitment of interneurons into dLGN and vLGN
source: Thus, SHH signaling appears critical for both thalamic Fgf15 expression and the recruitment of interneurons into dLGN and vLGN.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data from Shhfl/flNesCre mutants showing reduced Fgf15 and Gad1+ cells

claim: Ptch1, Smo, and Gli1 are expressed in visual thalamus at P3
source: Analysis of these data showed that three canonical SHH signaling components, Ptch1, Smo, and Gli1, are expressed in visual thalamus at P3 (Figure 2A), when Fgf15 expression is high in this region (Su et al., 2020).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNAseq data analysis shown in Figure 2A

claim: Gli1-tdT+ cells in visual thalamus express S100β
source: Immunostaining for S100ß, a commonly used marker for astrocytes, revealed S100ß expression in Gli1-tdT+ cells, suggesting that these astrocytes generate Gli1 (Figure 2C, D).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining shown in Figure 2C, D

claim: All Gli1-tdT+ cells express Gja1 mRNA in visual thalamus
source: In fact, we observed that Gja1 mRNA was present in all Gli1-tdT+ cells, suggesting expression of this transcription factor was specific to astrocytes in visual thalamus (Figure 2E, F).
evidence: Demonstrated by ISH data shown in Figure 2E, F with quantification showing 100% colocalization

claim: A high percentage of Aldh1l1-GFP+ astrocytes express Ptch1 and Smo in P3 dLGN and vLGN
source: ISH with riboprobes against Ptch1 and Smo revealed that a high percentage of Aldh1l1-GFP+astrocytes express these genes in P3 dLGN and vLGN (Figure 2G–J).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNAscope ISH data shown in Figure 2G–J

claim: Astrocytes in perinatal visual thalamus have the cellular machinery to respond to SHH
source: Together, these data demonstrate that astrocytes in perinatal visual thalamus have the cellular machinery to respond to SHH.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression of Ptch1, Smo, and Gli1 in thalamic astrocytes

claim: Shh mRNA expression is restricted to the GCL of the retina at P3
source: At P3, not only is Shh mRNA expression restricted to the GCL of the retina, but it is expressed by CALB2+ RGCs (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: Demonstrated by RNAscope ISH shown in Figure 3A, B

claim: At least 39 out of 41 RGC subtypes express Shh mRNA at P5
source: Two important observations were made through this analysis: (1) all RGC subtypes express high levels of Calb2, confirming the reliability of targeting this molecule to study RGCs (Kerr et al., 2019); (2) at least 39 out of 41 RGC subtypes express Shh mRNA (Figure 3C).
evidence: Demonstrated by reanalysis of single-cell RNAseq data from Rheaume et al., 2018, shown in Figure 3C

claim: RGCs in the developing postnatal retina express SHH
source: These results suggested that RGCs in the developing postnatal retina express SHH, which can potentially influence the role of thalamic astrocytes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ISH and single-cell RNAseq data showing Shh expression in RGCs

claim: There is active SHH signaling in dLGN and vLGN at P3
source: Here, staining for βGal in P3 Gli1nlacZ/+ mice demonstrated that when thalamic Fgf15 expression is high and interneuron migration occurs, there is indeed active SHH signaling in dLGN and vLGN (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by βGal staining in Gli1nlacZ/+ mice shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Shhfl/fl;Calb2Cre mutant mice are viable, fertile, and indistinguishable from littermate controls
source: Shhfl/fl;Calb2Cre mutant mice are viable, fertile, and indistinguishable from littermate controls.
evidence: This is a direct observation of the mutant mice

claim: There is a significant decrease in Shh mRNA in the retina of Shhfl/fl;Calb2Cre mutants
source: qRT-PCR analysis confirmed a significant decrease in Shh mRNA in the retina of these mutants (Figure 3E).
evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3E

claim: RGC axons from both eyes in Shhfl/fl;Calb2Cre mice are capable of innervating dLGN and form normal appearing eye-specific projections
source: Intraocular CTB injections showed that RGC axons from both eyes in Shhfl/fl;Calb2Cre mice are capable of innervating dLGN and form normal appearing eye-specific projections in this region (Figure 4).
evidence: Demonstrated by CTB labeling experiments shown in Figure 4

claim: There is a significant reduction of Fgf15+ cells in the dLGN and vLGN of P3 Shhfl/fl;Calb2Cre mutants
source: ISH analysis demonstrated a significant reduction of Fgf15+ cells in the dLGN and vLGN of P3 Shhfl/fl;Calb2Cre mutants (Figure 5A, B).
evidence: Demonstrated by ISH data shown in Figure 5A, B

claim: Loss of RGC-derived SHH does not impact the number of astrocytes in developing dLGN and vLGN
source: ISH analysis showed no significant difference in the distribution of Fgfr3-expressing cells between the controls and mutants (Figure 5C and D), suggesting that loss of RGC-derived SHH does not the impact number of astrocytes in developing dLGN and vLGN.
evidence: Demonstrated by ISH for Fgfr3 shown in Figure 5C, D

claim: SHH signaling from RGCs is necessary for astrocytic expression of Fgf15 in visual thalamus
source: These results demonstrate that SHH signaling from RGCs is not only necessary for astrocytic expression of Fgf15 in visual thalamus but that RGCs are the primary source of SHH to drive Fgf15 expression in thalamic astrocytes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing reduced Fgf15 in Shhfl/fl;Calb2Cre mutants

claim: There is a significant reduction in the percentage of Gad1-expressing cells in dLGN and vLGN of Shhfl/fl;Calb2Cre mice at P7
source: Our ISH data revealed that there was significant reduction in the percentage of Gad1-expressing cells in dLGN and vLGN of Shhfl/fl;Calb2Cre mice at P7 (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: Demonstrated by ISH data shown in Figure 6A, B

claim: There is a persistent, significant decrease in the percentage of Gad1-expressing cells in dLGN and vLGN of adult Shhfl/fl;Calb2Cre mutants
source: Indeed, our data revealed a persistent, significant decrease in the percentage of Gad1-expressing cells in dLGN and vLGN of adult mutants (Figure 6C and D), similar to what we have previously reported to occur in the visual thalamus of Fgf15−/− mutants (Su et al., 2020).
evidence: Demonstrated by ISH data shown in Figure 6C, D

claim: RGC axons play critical roles in the development of inhibitory circuits in visual thalamus
source: Axons of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) play critical roles in the development of inhibitory circuits in visual thalamus.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the overall findings of the study

claim: RGC axons signal astrocytes to induce the expression of FGF15
source: We previously reported that RGC axons signal astrocytes to induce the expression of fibroblast growth factor 15 (FGF15), a motogen required for GABAergic interneuron migration into visual thalamus.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Su et al., 2020)

claim: Thalamus-projecting RGCs express SHH
source: Specifically, we show that thalamus-projecting RGCs express SHH and thalamic astrocytes generate downstream components of SHH signaling.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the ISH and RNAseq data in the manuscript

claim: Deletion of RGC-derived SHH leads to a significant decrease in Fgf15 expression
source: Deletion of RGC-derived SHH leads to a significant decrease in Fgf15 expression, as well as in the percentage of interneurons recruited into visual thalamus.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data from Shhfl/fl;Calb2Cre mutants

claim: Retinal-derived sonic hedgehog (SHH) is essential for interneuron recruitment into visual thalamus
source: Instead, our data show that retinal-derived sonic hedgehog (SHH) is essential for interneuron recruitment.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on the data from Shhfl/fl;Calb2Cre mutants

claim: The dLGN is important for image-forming visual functions
source: Despite being adjacent, these nuclei have diverse roles in visual processing, with the dLGN being important for image-forming visual functions, and the vLGN and IGL contributing more to non-image-forming visual functions (such as visuomotor functions, circadian photoentrainment, and mood regulation) (Fratzl et al., 2021; Guido, 2018; Huang et al., 2019; Monavarfeshani et al., 2017; Salay and Huberman, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature

claim: The vLGN and IGL contribute to non-image-forming visual functions
source: Despite being adjacent, these nuclei have diverse roles in visual processing, with the dLGN being important for image-forming visual functions, and the vLGN and IGL contributing more to non-image-forming visual functions (such as visuomotor functions, circadian photoentrainment, and mood regulation) (Fratzl et al., 2021; Guido, 2018; Huang et al., 2019; Monavarfeshani et al., 2017; Salay and Huberman, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature

claim: The most abundant neurons in dLGN are glutamatergic thalamocortical relay cells
source: In fact, while the most abundant neurons in dLGN are glutamatergic thalamocortical relay cells, most neurons in vLGN are GABAergic and appear to represent a heterogeneous group of cell types with distinct morphologies, projections, and functions (Ciftcioglu et al., 2020; Crombie and Busse, 2021; Harrington, 1997; Yuge et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature

claim: Most neurons in vLGN are GABAergic
source: In fact, while the most abundant neurons in dLGN are glutamatergic thalamocortical relay cells, most neurons in vLGN are GABAergic and appear to represent a heterogeneous group of cell types with distinct morphologies, projections, and functions (Ciftcioglu et al., 2020; Crombie and Busse, 2021; Harrington, 1997; Yuge et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature

claim: A shared mechanism contributes to the recruitment and integration of GABAergic neurons into both dLGN and vLGN
source: In fact, a shared mechanism appears to exist that contributes to the recruitment and integration of these GABAergic neurons into both dLGN and vLGN (Golding et al., 2014; Su et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work

claim: The recruitment of migrating interneurons into the perinatal dLGN and vLGN requires the innervation of these regions by RGC axons
source: Specifically, the recruitment of migrating interneurons into the perinatal dLGN and vLGN requires the innervation of these regions by RGC axons.
evidence: This is supported by previous work cited in the manuscript

claim: The expression of FGF15 by thalamic astrocytes is dependent on retinal inputs
source: We reported that the expression of migratory cue fibroblast growth factor 15 (FGF15) by thalamic astrocytes is dependent on retinal inputs and the loss of this FGF leads to a reduction in the number of GABAergic interneurons in visual thalamus.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Su et al., 2020)

claim: The loss of FGF15 leads to a reduction in the number of GABAergic interneurons in visual thalamus
source: We reported that the expression of migratory cue fibroblast growth factor 15 (FGF15) by thalamic astrocytes is dependent on retinal inputs and the loss of this FGF leads to a reduction in the number of GABAergic interneurons in visual thalamus.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Su et al., 2020)

claim: The decreased number of GABAergic interneurons in the absence of FGF15 is not due to an increase in programmed cell death
source: The decreasd number of GABAergic interneurons in the absence of FGF15 is not due to an increase in programmed cell death.
evidence: This is stated based on previous findings

claim: In the absence of FGF15, GABAergic interneurons are misrouted into regions adjacent to the dorsal thalamus
source: Instead, these cells are misrouted into regions adjacent to the dorsal thalamus, specifically affecting their recruitment into dLGN and vLGN.
evidence: This is stated based on previous findings

claim: TeNT is a protease that cleaves Synaptobrevin2/VAMP2
source: TeNT is a protease that cleaves the vesicular SNARE Synaptobrevin2/VAMP2 (Syb2), which is required for the exocytosis of neurotransmitters (Link et al., 1992; Schoch et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature

claim: Synaptobrevin2/VAMP2 is required for the exocytosis of neurotransmitters
source: TeNT is a protease that cleaves the vesicular SNARE Synaptobrevin2/VAMP2 (Syb2), which is required for the exocytosis of neurotransmitters (Link et al., 1992; Schoch et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature

claim: Retinal inputs account for only 5–10% of the total synapses onto a dLGN relay cell
source: However, retinal inputs account for only 5–10% of the total synapses onto a dLGN relay cell (Bickford et al., 2010; Van Horn et al., 2000; Sherman and Guillery, 2002), making it difficult to detect significant changes in just a small fraction of the synapses in visual thalamus.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature

claim: RGC activity during perinatal development is critical for eye-specific segregation of retinal axons
source: RGC activity during perinatal development is critical for eye-specific segregation of retinal axons (Huberman et al., 2003; Penn et al., 1998; Pfeiffenberger et al., 2005), therefore, we assessed eye-specific RGC projections in Rosa26floxstop-TeNT;Calb2Cre mice.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature

claim: SHH signaling regulates morphogenesis, cell differentiation, and cell proliferation
source: SHH signaling has well established roles in regulating morphogenesis, cell differentiation, and cell proliferation (Garcia et al., 2018; Ishibashi and McMahon, 2002; Komada et al., 2008a; Marigo et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature

claim: In the embryonic retina, local expression of SHH is critical for promoting and maintaining the proliferation of retinal precursor cells
source: In the embryonic retina, local expression of SHH is critical for promoting and maintaining the proliferation of retinal precursor cells (Jensen and Wallace, 1997; Wang et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature

claim: RGC-derived SHH protein is anterogradely transported along axons
source: RGC-derived SHH protein has been shown to be anterogradely transported along axons, where it maintains the proliferative capacity of astrocytes in the optic nerve (Dakubo et al., 2008; Wallace and Raff, 1999) and acts as cue to guide eye-specific axon segregation at the optic chiasm (Peng et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature

claim: RGC-derived SHH maintains the proliferative capacity of astrocytes in the optic nerve
source: RGC-derived SHH protein has been shown to be anterogradely transported along axons, where it maintains the proliferative capacity of astrocytes in the optic nerve (Dakubo et al., 2008; Wallace and Raff, 1999) and acts as cue to guide eye-specific axon segregation at the optic chiasm (Peng et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature

claim: RGC-derived SHH acts as a cue to guide eye-specific axon segregation at the optic chiasm
source: RGC-derived SHH protein has been shown to be anterogradely transported along axons, where it maintains the proliferative capacity of astrocytes in the optic nerve (Dakubo et al., 2008; Wallace and Raff, 1999) and acts as cue to guide eye-specific axon segregation at the optic chiasm (Peng et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature

claim: Retina-derived SHH has been detected as far as the superior colliculus
source: Radiolabeling experiments have reported the presence of retina-derived SHH as far as the superior colliculus (Traiffort et al., 2001), a midbrain retinorecipient region, suggesting previously unexplored roles for RGC-derived SHH likely exist beyond the optic nerve and chiasm.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature

claim: Neuron-derived SHH directly acts on astrocytes residing in the target regions of their axonal projections
source: These results are in line with several recent studies with showing that neuron-derived SHH directly acts on astrocytes residing in the target regions of their axonal projections (Garcia et al., 2010; Hill et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature

claim: FGF15 expression is dependent on local SHH signaling in the embryonic brain
source: While FGF15 expression has been shown to be dependent on local SHH signaling in the embryonic brain (Ishibashi and McMahon, 2002; Kim et al., 2018; Komada et al., 2008b; Saitsu et al., 2005; Yabut et al., 2019), this is the first study to provide evidence for long-distance SHH signaling to regulate the expression of astrocyte-derived FGF15.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature

claim: This is the first study to provide evidence for long-distance SHH signaling to regulate the expression of astrocyte-derived FGF15
source: While FGF15 expression has been shown to be dependent on local SHH signaling in the embryonic brain (Ishibashi and McMahon, 2002; Kim et al., 2018; Komada et al., 2008b; Saitsu et al., 2005; Yabut et al., 2019), this is the first study to provide evidence for long-distance SHH signaling to regulate the expression of astrocyte-derived FGF15.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the current study's findings

claim: The loss of SHH signaling dramatically affects specific subtypes of GABAergic neurons in other brain regions
source: In other brain regions, the loss of SHH signaling has been observed to dramatically affect specific subtypes of GABAergic neurons, such as interneurons that express parvalbumin (Pvalb) or Somatostatin (Sst) (Ihrie et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2005), which may explain the partial loss of Gad1+ cells in the visual thalamus of Shhfl/fl;Calb2Cre mutants.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature

claim: Transcriptional, morphological, and functional studies have been unable to parse dLGN interneurons into more than one or two subtypes
source: In dLGN, transcriptional, morphological, and functional studies have been unable to parse interneurons into more than one or two subtypes (Charalambakis et al., 2019; Leist et al., 2016), making it difficult to study the specificity for loss of Gad1+ cells in this retinorecipient brain region.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature

claim: vLGN contains numerous transcriptionally distinct GABAergic cell types
source: In contrast, vLGN contains numerous transcriptionally distinct GABAergic cell types (including both local interneurons and projection neurons), some of which exhibit regional preferences, unique morphologies, and distinct connectivity (Fratzl et al., 2021; Sabbagh et al., 2021; Salay and Huberman, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature

claim: A more dramatic decrease in Gad1+ cells was observed in Shhfl/fl;NesCre mutants compared to Shhfl/fl;Calb2Cre or Atoh7−/− mice
source: It is also noteworthy that we observed more dramatic decrease in Gad1+ cells in Shhfl/fl;NesCre mutants, particularly in the vLGN, compared to the reduction observed in either Shhfl/fl;Calb2Cre or Atoh7−/− mice.
evidence: This is based on comparison of data from different mutant lines

claim: In Shhfl/fl;NesCre mutants, SHH loss occurs much earlier in development and in progenitor zones
source: In Shhfl/fl;NesCre mutants, SHH loss occurs much earlier in development and in progenitor zones (Lendahl et al., 1990; Zimmerman et al., 1994), likely impacting the generation of GABAergic progenitors that will eventually migrate into visual thalamus.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing and location of Cre expression in NesCre mice

claim: Shh null mice show defects in ventral patterning and a noticeable decrease in the size of their brain
source: Indeed, Shh null mice show defects in ventral patterning and a noticeable decrease in the size of their brain (Chiang et al., 1996; Machold et al., 2003; Rallu et al., 2002), indicating key roles for this morphogen in many aspects of early brain development.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature

claim: SHH is necessary for maintenance of astrocyte proliferation in the optic nerve
source: In the optic nerve, SHH has been reported to be necessary for maintenance of astrocyte proliferation (Dakubo et al., 2008; Wallace and Raff, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature

claim: Only a small fraction of astrocytes express Fgf15 in visual thalamus
source: However, only a small fraction of astrocytes express Fgf15 in visual thalamus (Su et al., 2020), raising the questions of whether only some thalamic astrocytes generate the machinery to respond to SHH or whether retina-derived SHH itself can alter the identity of thalamic astrocytes to generate heterogeneity in these cells.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work

claim: Neuron-derived SHH is integral for maintaining the identity of Bergmann glial cells
source: In support of the latter possibility, neuron-derived SHH is integral for maintaining the identity of Bergmann glial cells, a specialized astrocyte type in the cerebellum (Farmer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature

claim: A much greater proportion of astrocytes in visual thalamus generate SHH signaling components Ptch1 and Smo compared to those that generate Fgf15
source: However, it is important to note that we found that a much greater proportion of astrocytes in visual thalamus generate SHH signaling components, Ptch1 and Smo, compared to those that generate Fgf15.
evidence: This is based on the data presented in the manuscript

claim: SHH appears to be important for a variety of astrocytic functions including modulation of neuronal activity, regulation of energy metabolism, and neuroprotection
source: Outside of the thalamus, SHH appears to be important for a variety of astrocytic functions, including modulation of neuronal activity (Hill et al., 2019), regulation of energy metabolism (Tirou et al., 2021), and neuroprotection (Ugbode et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature

claim: Many developmental aspects underlying orderly connections in the mammalian visual system are dependent on retinal activity even before eye opening
source: Many developmental aspects underlying orderly connections in the mammalian visual system are dependent on retinal activity even before eye opening (D'Souza and Lang, 2020; Huberman et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature

claim: Application of tetrodotoxin in neonatal organotypic thalamic slices led to the suggestion that activity was necessary for directing the spatial incorporation of interneurons into dLGN circuits
source: Application of tetrodotoxin in neonatal organotypic thalamic slices led to the suggestion that activity was necessary for directing the spatial incorporation of these interneurons into dLGN circuits (Golding et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature

claim: Activity in hippocampal neurons causes the release of SHH in a SNAREs- and Ca2+-dependent manner
source: Although such roles of neuronal stimulation on SHH release have not been reported in visual thalamus, activity in hippocampal neurons has been shown to cause the release of SHH in a SNAREs- and Ca2+-dependent manner (Su et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature

claim: Retinal inputs have both activity-dependent and activity-independent roles in orchestrating the development of visual thalamus
source: Overall, this suggests that retinal inputs have both activity-dependent and activity-independent roles in orchestrating the development of visual thalamus.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings that activity blockade does not affect interneuron recruitment but SHH deletion does

claim: FGF15 has reduced heparin-binding affinity compared to other FGFs
source: Specifically, thalamic astrocytes generate the motogen FGF15, which in contrast to other FGFs has reduced heparin-binding affinity (Ornitz and Itoh, 2015) making it an ideal guidance cue for long-distance migration of interneurons (Golding et al., 2014; Jager et al., 2016; Jager et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature

claim: FGFR3 is not a major receptor for FGF15
source: It is important to point out for clarity that FGFR3 is not a major receptor for FGF15 (Ornitz and Itoh, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature

claim: RGCs are the primary source of SHH to drive Fgf15 expression in thalamic astrocytes
source: These results demonstrate that SHH signaling from RGCs is not only necessary for astrocytic expression of Fgf15 in visual thalamus but that RGCs are the primary source of SHH to drive Fgf15 expression in thalamic astrocytes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data from Shhfl/fl;Calb2Cre mutants showing reduced Fgf15

claim: The findings identify a morphogen-dependent neuron–astrocyte signaling mechanism essential for the migration of thalamic interneurons
source: Overall, our findings identify a morphogen-dependent neuron–astrocyte signaling mechanism essential for the migration of thalamic interneurons.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study

claim: S100β immunohistochemistry labels a small population of microglia in visual thalamus
source: However, we recently reported that S100ß immunohistochemistry (IHC) also labels a small population of microglia in visual thalamus (Somaiya et al., 2021), therefore, we confirmed that tdT+ cells were astrocytes by ISH for Gja1, the gene encoding Connexin 43.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work

claim: At least 40 transcriptionally distinct types of RGCs exist in the mouse retina
source: Since at least 40 transcriptionally distinct types of RGCs exist in the mouse retina (Tran et al., 2019), we sought to identify whether all RGCs generate Shh mRNA (which looked to be the case based on ISH, Figure 3A) or whether specific RGC subtypes generate this morphogen in the perinatal retina.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature

claim: All RGC subtypes express high levels of Calb2
source: Two important observations were made through this analysis: (1) all RGC subtypes express high levels of Calb2, confirming the reliability of targeting this molecule to study RGCs (Kerr et al., 2019); (2) at least 39 out of 41 RGC subtypes express Shh mRNA (Figure 3C).
evidence: Demonstrated by reanalysis of single-cell RNAseq data shown in Figure 3C

claim: RGCs show no to very low expression of Calb2 before E16
source: Multiple reasons led us to choose Calb2Cre mice to target RGC-derived SHH: (1) Shh and Calb2 are coexpressed in RGC subtypes (Figure 3C); (2) RGCs show no to very low expression of Calb2 before E16 (Shekhar et al., 2022), suggesting that Shhfl/fl;Calb2Cre mutant mice will retain other known Shh functions (Wang et al., 2005) in early embryonic retina (Figure 3D);
evidence: This is supported by citation and data shown in Figure 3D

claim: CALB2+ cells are largely absent from the neonatal and postnatal dLGN
source: we previously reported that CALB2+ cells are largely absent from the neonatal and postnatal dLGN and are only sparsely distributed in vLGN at these ages (Su et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work

claim: Only a limited number of CALB2+ cells are present in the thalamic and tectal progenitor zones
source: Here, we add to these points by showing only a limited number of CALB2+ cells are present in the thalamic and tectal progenitor zones that are thought to give rise to these sets of migrating interneurons (Golding et al., 2014; Jager et al., 2016; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by IHC data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2
